question: At an equal candidate budget, do QAOA samples from IBM hardware lead to better retrained pruned networks than classical candidate generators?
encoding: qubit q keeps group 2q if bit=0 else group 2q+1; all 2^100 bitstrings are valid; 50% of neurons kept
training: fashion_v2.train: 20 epochs, Adam lr 0.003, batch 256, paired shuffles; rewind to original init
qubo: ridge (RidgeCV alphas logspace(-4,3,15), 5-fold) on 100 linear + chip-edge pairwise features; target = validation loss
angle_tuning: exact p=1 light-cone expectation; 41x41 grid then Nelder-Mead

methods.Simulated annealing (matched): 16 chains x 256 single-flip steps = 4096 QUBO evaluations; all visited states are candidates
methods.Simulated annealing (long): 64 chains x 20000 steps = 1,280,000 QUBO evaluations (reference ceiling); candidates = states in the final 2000 steps

pick_rule: the 10 distinct candidates with the lowest QUBO score
primary_metric: best-of-10 validation loss after retraining (lower is better)
win_rule: QAOA beats a method if its best-of-10 validation loss is lower in at least 2 of 3 seeds AND its mean best-of-10 validation loss over the 3 seeds is lower
secondary: mean validation loss of the 10 picks
mean QUBO score of all candidates
share of candidates better than the best of 4096 random samples
hardware vs ideal expected QUBO score
test accuracy of each method's best pick (reported once, never used to choose)
everything_reported: all seeds, all methods, all jobs, including failures
known_caveats: The native 100-qubit region has 100 couplings (nearly a tree), so the QUBO is easy for classical solvers; the test is about candidate quality at equal budget, not about beating the best classical solver.
Restricting each qubit to a choice between two fixed groups searches 2^100 of the C(200,100) possible half-size networks.
p=1 QAOA is the shallowest version; it was chosen so angles can be tuned exactly without simulating 100 qubits.
Three seeds and one fixed data split: a demonstration-scale test, not a general benchmark.
